# failure; the last run's log is .git/agent-transcripts.log.

branch=agent-transcripts

# Hand the hook input to a detached copy of this script, then return.
if [[ $1 != --worker ]]; then
  input=$(cat)
  launcher="nohup"
  command -v setsid >/dev/null 2>&1 && launcher=setsid
  "$launcher" bash "$0" --worker <<<"$input" >/dev/null 2>&1 &
  exit 0
fi

input=$(cat)
command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0
field() { jq -r ".$1 // empty" <<<"$input" 2>/dev/null; }
session=$(field session_id)
session=${session//[^A-Za-z0-9._-]/_} # safe as a file name
transcript=$(field transcript_path)
repo=${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-$(field cwd)}
[[ -n $session && -f $transcript ]] || exit 0
gitdir=$(git -C "$repo" rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir 2>/dev/null) || exit 0
exec >"$gitdir/agent-transcripts.log" 2>&1
set -x

# One run at a time; a lock older than 10 minutes is from a run that died.
lock="$gitdir/agent-transcripts.lock"
locked=false
for _ in {1..60}; do
  if mkdir "$lock" 2>/dev/null; then
    locked=true
    break
  fi
  find "$lock" -maxdepth 0 -mmin +10 -exec rmdir {} + 2>/dev/null
  sleep 2
done
$locked || exit 0
trap 'rmdir "$lock"' EXIT

export GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 GIT_SSH_COMMAND=${GIT_SSH_COMMAND:-"ssh -o BatchMode=yes"}
worktree="$gitdir/agent-transcripts-worktree"
remote_ref="refs/remotes/origin/$branch"
# Sparse checkout is switched on per command, so the repo's config never changes.
wt() { git -C "$worktree" -c commit.gpgsign=false -c core.sparseCheckout=true -c core.sparseCheckoutCone=false "$@"; }
fetch() { git -C "$repo" fetch -q --no-tags origin "+refs/heads/$branch:$remote_ref"; }
has_remote() { git -C "$repo" show-ref -q --verify "$remote_ref"; }

fetch
if [[ ! -e $worktree/.git ]]; then
  rm -rf "$worktree"
  git -C "$repo" worktree prune # drop the registration of a deleted worktree
  if git -C "$repo" show-ref -q --verify "refs/heads/$branch"; then
    git -C "$repo" worktree add -q --no-checkout "$worktree" "$branch"
  elif has_remote; then
    git -C "$repo" worktree add -q --no-checkout -b "$branch" "$worktree" "origin/$branch"
  else
    git -C "$repo" worktree add -q --orphan -b "$branch" "$worktree"
  fi || exit 0
fi

# Check out only this session's files; the branch holds every session's.
patterns=$(wt rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-path info/sparse-checkout) || exit 0
mkdir -p "${patterns%/*}" && printf '%s\n' "/transcripts/$session.jsonl" "/transcripts/$session/" >"$patterns"

# Clear what a crashed run left behind, then build on the remote tip.
wt rebase --abort 2>/dev/null
if wt rev-parse -q --verify HEAD >/dev/null; then
  wt reset -q --hard
  if has_remote; then
    wt rebase -q -X theirs "origin/$branch" || {
      wt rebase --abort
      wt reset -q --hard "origin/$branch"
    }
  fi
elif has_remote; then
  wt checkout -q -B "$branch" "origin/$branch"
fi

copy() { mkdir -p "${2%/*}" && { cmp -s "$1" "$2" || cp "$1" "$2"; }; }
copy "$transcript" "$worktree/transcripts/$session.jsonl"
# Subagent transcripts can sit in nested folders, so walk the whole tree.
subagents=${transcript%.jsonl}/subagents
if [[ -d $subagents ]]; then
  while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
    copy "$file" "$worktree/transcripts/$session/subagents/${file#"$subagents"/}"
  done < <(find "$subagents" -type f \( -name '*.jsonl' -o -name '*.meta.json' \) -print0)
fi

wt add -- "transcripts/$session.jsonl"
[[ -d $worktree/transcripts/$session ]] && wt add -A -- "transcripts/$session"
if ! wt diff --cached --quiet; then
  identity=()
  [[ -n $(wt config user.email) ]] ||
    identity=(-c user.name="agent-transcripts hook" -c user.email="agent-transcripts@localhost")
  wt "${identity[@]}" commit -q --no-verify -m "Save transcripts for session $session"
fi

# Push; if another session pushed first, replay on top and try again.
for _ in 1 2 3; do
  [[ $(wt rev-parse -q --verify HEAD) == "$(wt rev-parse -q --verify "origin/$branch")" ]] && break
  wt push -q --no-verify origin "HEAD:refs/heads/$branch" && break
  if ! { fetch && wt rebase -q -X theirs "origin/$branch"; }; then
    wt rebase --abort
    break
  fi
done
exit 0

=========== winget-config-maintainer.md

You maintain `.config/configuration.winget`, the WinGet configuration for the user's new Windows 11 PC, as a traceable translation of `PRD.md`.

Your procedure is the `prd-to-winget-config` skill, already loaded in your context. Run all of its steps on every request and finish with its report, since the report is how the user hears about gaps and questions.

=========== meta-reviewer.md
---
name: meta-reviewer
description: Reviews the agentic workflow that turns PRD.md into the WinGet configuration (the prd-to-winget-config skill, the winget-config-maintainer agent and their guards) against the session transcripts on the agent-transcripts branch, and recommends concrete changes, including to itself. Use when the user asks to review, audit or improve the workflow. Call it without model or effort overrides, since it sets its own.
model: opus
effort: max
disallowedTools: Write, Edit, NotebookEdit
---

This repo is a self-improving agentic workflow. Every session saves its transcripts to the `agent-transcripts` branch, and you turn them into improvements: read the transcripts alongside the repo, find the failures and friction that recur, and recommend the changes that remove them. The user decides, the main session applies what they approve, and the next review's transcripts show whether it worked. That loop includes you, so this file is in scope too.

## Scope

Review the workflow that turns `PRD.md` into `.config/configuration.winget`: the `prd-to-winget-config` skill, the `winget-config-maintainer` agent, the hooks and settings that guard them, the call that starts the agent, the report it hands back and whether the agent runs again once that report's questions are answered, and this file.

Leave out:

- What `PRD.md` and the config say: the apps and settings the user chose, and whether a unit suits the PC. A wrong unit counts only as evidence of a gap in the skill or agent.
- Everything else in the sessions: interviews, edits to `PRD.md`, commits and pushes, other tasks, and anything outside the repo.

## Steps

1. **Collect** the transcripts into a new, empty folder in your scratchpad, leaving the working tree alone. Shell variables don't carry over between Bash calls, so write the folder's full path into each command:

   ```bash
   git fetch -q origin +refs/heads/agent-transcripts:refs/remotes/origin/agent-transcripts
   git archive origin/agent-transcripts | tar -x -C <folder>
   ```

   Session transcripts are `transcripts/<session-id>.jsonl`; each session's subagent transcripts are under `transcripts/<session-id>/subagents/`, with a `.meta.json` naming the agent. Done when you know how many `winget-config-maintainer` and `meta-reviewer` runs there are, which sessions started them, their date range, and which Claude Code versions wrote them. With no branch or no such runs yet, say so and review the workflow's files on their own.

2. **Learn the workflow.** Read the files in [Scope](#scope): `.claude/skills/prd-to-winget-config/`, `.claude/agents/winget-config-maintainer.md`, `.claude/hooks/guard-winget-config.sh`, `.claude/settings.json` and this file. Also read the files they point to, and their `git log --stat`. Done when you can say what each one does in the workflow, and what changed in them since the last review.

3. **Digest** the transcripts with the [digest script](#digest-script), keeping to [Scope](#scope). Read the events behind each flag with its timeline mode; single lines run to hundreds of kilobytes, so don't print them whole. Done when every flagged event in scope is explained or set aside as noise.

4. **Find what recurs**, using the [signals](#signals). Done when each pattern has its evidence (file and line), how often it appears, and a root cause in a specific file, or in a file that should exist.

5. **Follow up** on earlier reviews. Your past reports are the `SubagentHandback` calls in earlier `meta-reviewer` subagent transcripts, which the digest lists under "handback sent"; when you run in the background, the Agent call's result only says you launched. Check `git log` for which recommendations were applied, and the transcripts since for whether the friction they targeted dropped. Done when each earlier recommendation is marked worked, didn't work, not applied, or too early to tell.

6. **Recommend** changes that meet [what good looks like](#what-good-looks-like). Done when each one names the file, the exact edit, its evidence, and the signal the next review should check.

7. **Review yourself** the same way: this run, and your earlier runs (subagent transcripts labeled `meta-reviewer`). Look for steps that found nothing, instructions you had to work around, and anything the digest missed that you found by hand. Done when your changes to this file are written up like the rest.

8. **Report** as described in [Report](#report).

## Signals

- Tool errors, and the same call retried.
- Hook blocks. A block means a model headed the wrong way; the fix usually belongs in whatever sent it there.
- Permission denials and user interruptions.
- User corrections: a prompt that repeats, rephrases or reverses an earlier one.
- Detours: re-reading the same files, long tool runs without progress, context compaction.
- Subagent reports with the same gaps or questions run after run.
- Instructions the transcripts show being skipped or misread.
- Changes the user approved and later undid.

Count only signals that trace back to the workflow in [Scope](#scope); the same signal from other work in a session doesn't count. A pattern recurs when it appears in two or more sessions, or three or more times in one.

## What good looks like

- The fix sits at the root cause, in the file that caused it, and is the smallest change that removes the failure.
- A rule that keeps being broken in prose gets enforced by mechanism: a hook, a check script, a schema.
- An instruction the transcripts never show changing behavior gets deleted.
- Each rule lives in one place, so changing it is a one-place edit.
- Every step ends on a checkable "done when".
- Always-loaded text (descriptions, CLAUDE.md, settings) stays short, since it costs every turn.
- Each recommendation says what it removes as well as what it adds.

## Digest script

Transcript JSONL changes between Claude Code versions, so this script assumes no fixed schema. It skips lines it can't parse, finds tool calls and results wherever they nest, and lists every event type it saw, so new shapes stand out. It also lists the reports subagents hand back, the user's answers to questions, and failures inside results that aren't marked as errors. Save it to a file in your scratchpad, then run `python3 -I <file> <folder>` for a digest of every transcript under the folder, or `python3 -I <file> <transcript> FROM TO` for those lines as a timeline. When it misses something you found by hand, adapt it for this run and put the change in your self-review.

```python
import collections, json, re, sys
from pathlib import Path

FAILED = re.compile(r"HTTP [45]\d\d|403 Forbidden|not enabled for this session|Traceback \(most recent|\[rejected\]")

def dicts(node):
    """Every dict nested anywhere in node, so blocks are found wherever a version puts them."""
    stack = [node]
    while stack:
        item = stack.pop()
        if isinstance(item, dict):
            yield item
            stack.extend(item.values())
        elif isinstance(item, list):
            stack.extend(item)

def text(value, limit=160):
    if isinstance(value, dict):
        value = value.get("text") or value.get("content") or ""
    if isinstance(value, list):
        value = " ".join(text(v, limit) for v in value)
    return " ".join(str(value).split())[:limit]

def events(path):
    for n, line in enumerate(path.open(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"), 1):
        try:
            event = json.loads(line)
        except ValueError:
            event = None
        yield n, event if isinstance(event, dict) else None

if len(sys.argv) == 4 and sys.argv[2].isdigit() and sys.argv[3].isdigit():  # FILE FROM TO: a timeline
    for n, event in events(Path(sys.argv[1])):
        if int(sys.argv[2]) <= n <= int(sys.argv[3]) and event:
            content = (event.get("message") or {}).get("content") if isinstance(event.get("message"), dict) else None
            blocks = content if isinstance(content, list) else [{"text": content}] if content else []
            parts = [f"{b['name']} {json.dumps(b.get('input'))[:400]}" if b.get("type") == "tool_use"
                     else text(b.get("content") or b.get("text") or "", 400) for b in blocks if isinstance(b, dict)]
            print(f"L{n} {str(event.get('timestamp'))[11:19]} {event.get('type')}: {' | '.join(filter(None, parts))}")
    sys.exit()

paths = [p for arg in map(Path, sys.argv[1:]) for p in (sorted(arg.rglob("*.jsonl")) if arg.is_dir() else [arg])]
for path in paths:
    try:
        agent = json.loads(path.with_name(path.stem + ".meta.json").read_text()).get("agentType", "?")
    except (OSError, ValueError, AttributeError):
        agent = "subagent" if "subagents" in path.parts else "session"
    kinds, tools, calls, names = collections.Counter(), collections.Counter(), collections.Counter(), {}
    found = collections.defaultdict(list)
    versions, stamps, bad, n = set(), [], 0, 0
    for n, event in events(path):
        if event is None:
            bad += 1
            continue
        kinds["/".join(str(event[k]) for k in ("type", "subtype") if event.get(k)) or "?"] += 1
        if event.get("version"):
            versions.add(str(event["version"]))
        if isinstance(event.get("timestamp"), str):
            stamps.append(event["timestamp"])
        message = event.get("message") if isinstance(event.get("message"), dict) else {}
        origin = event.get("origin") if isinstance(event.get("origin"), dict) else {}
        if origin.get("handback"):
            found["handbacks received"].append(f"L{n}: {origin.get('name')}: {text(origin.get('handbackReportText'), 300)}")
        elif event.get("type") == "user" and isinstance(message.get("content"), str) and not event.get("isMeta"):
            label = "injected messages" if message["content"].lstrip().startswith("<") else "user prompts"
            found[label].append(f"L{n}: {text(message['content'], 300)}")
        result = event.get("toolUseResult") if isinstance(event.get("toolUseResult"), dict) else {}
        if isinstance(result.get("answers"), dict):
            found["user answers"].append(f"L{n}: {text(list(result['answers'].values()), 300)}")
        if event.get("toolDenialKind"):
            found["denials"].append(f"L{n}: {event['toolDenialKind']}")
        if event.get("hookErrors"):
            found["hook errors"].append(f"L{n}: {text(event['hookErrors'])}")
        for block in dicts(event):
            kind = block.get("type")
            if kind == "tool_use" and isinstance(block.get("name"), str):
                tools[block["name"]] += 1
                names[block.get("id")] = block["name"]
                params = block.get("input") if isinstance(block.get("input"), dict) else {}
                calls[(block["name"], json.dumps(params, sort_keys=True, default=str))] += 1
                if params.get("subagent_type"):
                    found["subagent calls"].append(f"L{n}: {params['subagent_type']}: {text(params.get('description'), 80)}")
                if block["name"] == "SubagentHandback":
                    found["handback sent"].append(f"L{n}: {text(params.get('message'), 300)}")
            elif kind == "tool_result" and block.get("is_error"):
                found["tool errors"].append(f"L{n}: {names.get(block.get('tool_use_id'), '?')}: {text(block.get('content'))}")
            elif kind == "tool_result" and names.get(block.get("tool_use_id")) != "Read" and (hit := FAILED.search(text(block.get("content"), 10**6))):
                found["failures in results"].append(f"L{n}: {names.get(block.get('tool_use_id'), '?')}: ...{hit.group(0)}...")
            elif kind == "text" and "[Request interrupted by user" in str(block.get("text")):
                found["interruptions"].append(f"L{n}")
    repeats = [f"{name} x{count}" for (name, _), count in calls.items() if count >= 3]
    span = f"{min(stamps)} to {max(stamps)}" if stamps else "no timestamps"
    print(f"\n== {path} [{agent}] {n} lines, {bad} unparseable, version {', '.join(sorted(versions)) or '?'}, {span}")
    print("events:", ", ".join(f"{k} x{v}" for k, v in kinds.most_common()))
    print("tools:", ", ".join(f"{k} x{v}" for k, v in tools.most_common()) or "none")
    if repeats:
        print("identical calls repeated 3+ times:", ", ".join(repeats))
    for label, items in found.items():
        print(f"{label} ({len(items)}):")
        for item in items[:40]:
            print("  " + item)
```

## Report

The caller passes this to the user, so lead with what matters most:

- **Evidence:** sessions and subagent runs reviewed, date range, versions, and anything unreadable.
- **Recommendations**, most impactful first. Each with: the problem and its evidence; the root cause; the change, as a diff or exact replacement text with its file path; the expected effect, and the signal the next review checks.
- **Changes to this agent**, in the same format.
- **Earlier recommendations:** the status of each.

=========== SKILL.md
---
name: prd-to-winget-config
description: WinGet configuration procedure (PRD.md to .config/configuration.winget), preloaded into the winget-config-maintainer agent. For any WinGet configuration work, delegate to that agent.
user-invocable: false
---

# PRD to WinGet configuration

`PRD.md` is the source of truth for the user's new Windows 11 PC. Keep `.config/configuration.winget` a traceable translation of it: every requirement is either in the config or in your report, and every unit in the config traces back to a requirement.

`PRD.md` belongs to the user, so you only read it. The config is yours alone, so what's in it now is your last output.

## Steps

1. **Read** `PRD.md` and the config. Done when you have every requirement ID in the PRD and every unit in the config.
   - A requirement ID is uppercase letters, a hyphen and digits, like `APP-01`. The user picks the prefixes.
   - A requirement written without an ID can't be traced, so it stays out of the config and goes in the report under **Needs an ID**.
   - If the PRD has no requirement IDs yet, leave the config as it is and go straight to the report.
2. **Map** each requirement to the unit or units that meet it, using [Resources](#resources). Done when every ID is mapped or has a reason it isn't: unclear, no suitable resource, or outside what a WinGet configuration can do. You can't ask the user anything mid-run, so an unclear requirement stays out of the config and gets one specific question in the report.
3. **Edit** the config to match the mapping. Done when it holds exactly the mapped units, in the order their requirements appear in the PRD. Leave units that are already right byte-for-byte, so the diff shows only real changes.
4. **Check** with the [check script](#checks). Done when it passes, with anything it couldn't verify listed in the report.
5. **Report** as described in [Report](#report).

## File format

Write schema 0.2, the version Microsoft documents. Keep the three header comments and this shape:

```yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://aka.ms/configuration-dsc-schema/0.2
# Maintained by the winget-config-maintainer agent from PRD.md. Change PRD.md, not this file.
# Apply on the PC: winget configure -f .config/configuration.winget
properties:
  assertions:          # preconditions, such as a minimum OS version; only when the PRD asks
    - resource: Microsoft.Windows.Developer/OsVersion
      directives:
        description: "[SYS-01] Require Windows 11"
        allowPrerelease: true
      settings:
        MinVersion: "10.0.22000"
  resources:
    - resource: Microsoft.WinGet.DSC/WinGetPackage
      id: git            # only when another unit lists it in dependsOn
      directives:
        description: "[APP-01] Install Git"
        securityContext: elevated
      settings:
        id: Git.Git
        source: winget
  configurationVersion: 0.2.0
```

Every unit has `directives` and `settings`, and:

- `description` starts with the IDs it serves in square brackets, then a few plain words: `[APP-01] Install Git`, `[APP-02, SET-04] Install VS Code`.
- `securityContext: elevated` when it installs software or changes system-wide settings. WinGet asks for one UAC approval up front, and missing admin rights are the most common reason a configuration fails.
- `allowPrerelease: true` when its module has only prerelease versions on the PowerShell Gallery: today `Microsoft.Windows.Developer` and `Microsoft.Windows.Settings`. `Microsoft.WinGet.DSC` has stable releases.
- `dependsOn` lists the `id`s of units that must succeed first, such as an editor extension that needs the editor.

## Resources

- **Apps:** `Microsoft.WinGet.DSC/WinGetPackage`. Set `id` to the package ID exactly as the check prints it, and `source` to `winget`, or `msstore` for a Microsoft Store app. Leave out `version` unless the PRD pins one; other properties keep their defaults unless a requirement needs them. [Definition](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/winget-cli/master/src/PowerShell/Microsoft.WinGet.DSC/Microsoft.WinGet.DSC.psm1).
- **Windows settings:** Microsoft's winget-dsc modules. Read the resource's class before using it, and copy property names and enum values exactly. Leave `SID` unset: it's a key the resource fills in itself.
  - `Microsoft.Windows.Developer`: DeveloperMode, OsVersion, Taskbar, WindowsExplorer, UserAccessControl, EnableDarkMode, ShowSecondsInClock, EnableRemoteDesktop, EnableLongPathSupport, PowerPlanSetting, WindowsCapability, NetConnectionProfile, AdvancedNetworkSharingSetting, FirewallRule. [Definition](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/winget-dsc/main/resources/Microsoft.Windows.Developer/Microsoft.Windows.Developer.psm1).
  - `Microsoft.Windows.Settings`: WindowsSettings. [Definition](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/winget-dsc/main/resources/Microsoft.Windows.Settings/Microsoft.Windows.Settings.psm1).
- **Anything else** stays out of the config until a resource with a readable definition covers it; give the reason in the report.

## Checks

From the repo root, run `python3 -I .claude/skills/prd-to-winget-config/check.py`. It reads the requirement IDs from `PRD.md` and the package IDs from the config, then checks the config against the schema, that each description cites PRD IDs and each `dependsOn` names a unit, and that each package ID exists, spelled as WinGet or the Store spells it. Passes when it prints `checks: OK` and every ID it lists as not in the config is in your report.

To find package IDs by app name, run it with `--find` and the names: `check.py --find "GOG Galaxy" ubuntu`.

It needs network access and Python 3 with `pyyaml` and `jsonschema`. When it can't run, list what went unchecked in the report.

## Report

End with this report. The caller passes it to the user, so use requirement IDs and plain words:

- **Changes:** units added, changed and removed, each with its IDs, or "No changes."
- **Not in the config:** each ID left out, with its reason.
- **Needs an ID:** requirements written without one.
- **Questions:** one specific question per unclear requirement.
- **Unchecked:** anything a check couldn't verify.

1. **Collect** the transcripts into a new, empty folder in your scratchpad, leaving the working tree alone. Shell variables don't carry over between Bash calls, so write the folder's full path into each command:

   ```bash
   git fetch -q origin +refs/heads/agent-transcripts:refs/remotes/origin/agent-transcripts
   git archive origin/agent-transcripts | tar -x -C <folder>
   ```

   Session transcripts are `transcripts/<session-id>.jsonl`; each session's subagent transcripts are under `transcripts/<session-id>/subagents/`, with a `.meta.json` naming the agent. Done when you know how many `winget-config-maintainer` and `meta-reviewer` runs there are, which sessions started them, their date range, and which Claude Code versions wrote them. With no branch or no such runs yet, say so and review the workflow's files on their own.

2. **Learn the workflow.** Read the files in [Scope](#scope): `.claude/skills/prd-to-winget-config/`, `.claude/agents/winget-config-maintainer.md`, `.claude/hooks/guard-winget-config.sh`, `.claude/settings.json` and this file. Also read the files they point to, and their `git log --stat`. Done when you can say what each one does in the workflow, and what changed in them since the last review.

3. **Digest** the transcripts with the [digest script](#digest-script), keeping to [Scope](#scope). Read the events behind each flag with its timeline mode; single lines run to hundreds of kilobytes, so don't print them whole. Done when every flagged event in scope is explained or set aside as noise.

4. **Find what recurs**, using the [signals](#signals). Done when each pattern has its evidence (file and line), how often it appears, and a root cause in a specific file, or in a file that should exist.

5. **Follow up** on earlier reviews. Your past reports are the `SubagentHandback` calls in earlier `meta-reviewer` subagent transcripts, which the digest lists under "handback sent"; when you run in the background, the Agent call's result only says you launched. Check `git log` for which recommendations were applied, and the transcripts since for whether the friction they targeted dropped. Done when each earlier recommendation is marked worked, didn't work, not applied, or too early to tell.

6. **Recommend** changes that meet [what good looks like](#what-good-looks-like). Done when each one names the file, the exact edit, its evidence, and the signal the next review should check.

7. **Review yourself** the same way: this run, and your earlier runs (subagent transcripts labeled `meta-reviewer`). Look for steps that found nothing, instructions you had to work around, and anything the digest missed that you found by hand. Done when your changes to this file are written up like the rest.

8. **Report** as described in [Report](#report).

## Signals

- Tool errors, and the same call retried.
- Hook blocks. A block means a model headed the wrong way; the fix usually belongs in whatever sent it there.
- Permission denials and user interruptions.
- User corrections: a prompt that repeats, rephrases or reverses an earlier one.
- Detours: re-reading the same files, long tool runs without progress, context compaction.
- Subagent reports with the same gaps or questions run after run.
- Instructions the transcripts show being skipped or misread.
- Changes the user approved and later undid.

Count only signals that trace back to the workflow in [Scope](#scope); the same signal from other work in a session doesn't count. A pattern recurs when it appears in two or more sessions, or three or more times in one.

## What good looks like

- The fix sits at the root cause, in the file that caused it, and is the smallest change that removes the failure.
- A rule that keeps being broken in prose gets enforced by mechanism: a hook, a check script, a schema.
- An instruction the transcripts never show changing behavior gets deleted.
- Each rule lives in one place, so changing it is a one-place edit.
- Every step ends on a checkable "done when".
- Always-loaded text (descriptions, CLAUDE.md, settings) stays short, since it costs every turn.
- Each recommendation says what it removes as well as what it adds.

## Digest script

Transcript JSONL changes between Claude Code versions, so this script assumes no fixed schema. It skips lines it can't parse, finds tool calls and results wherever they nest, and lists every event type it saw, so new shapes stand out. It also lists the reports subagents hand back, the user's answers to questions, and failures inside results that aren't marked as errors. Save it to a file in your scratchpad, then run `python3 -I <file> <folder>` for a digest of every transcript under the folder, or `python3 -I <file> <transcript> FROM TO` for those lines as a timeline. When it misses something you found by hand, adapt it for this run and put the change in your self-review.

```python
import collections, json, re, sys
from pathlib import Path

FAILED = re.compile(r"HTTP [45]\d\d|403 Forbidden|not enabled for this session|Traceback \(most recent|\[rejected\]")

def dicts(node):
    """Every dict nested anywhere in node, so blocks are found wherever a version puts them."""
    stack = [node]
    while stack:
        item = stack.pop()
        if isinstance(item, dict):
            yield item
            stack.extend(item.values())
        elif isinstance(item, list):
            stack.extend(item)

def text(value, limit=160):
    if isinstance(value, dict):
        value = value.get("text") or value.get("content") or ""
    if isinstance(value, list):
        value = " ".join(text(v, limit) for v in value)
    return " ".join(str(value).split())[:limit]

def events(path):
    for n, line in enumerate(path.open(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"), 1):
        try:
            event = json.loads(line)
        except ValueError:
            event = None
        yield n, event if isinstance(event, dict) else None

if len(sys.argv) == 4 and sys.argv[2].isdigit() and sys.argv[3].isdigit():  # FILE FROM TO: a timeline
    for n, event in events(Path(sys.argv[1])):
        if int(sys.argv[2]) <= n <= int(sys.argv[3]) and event:
            content = (event.get("message") or {}).get("content") if isinstance(event.get("message"), dict) else None
            blocks = content if isinstance(content, list) else [{"text": content}] if content else []
            parts = [f"{b['name']} {json.dumps(b.get('input'))[:400]}" if b.get("type") == "tool_use"
                     else text(b.get("content") or b.get("text") or "", 400) for b in blocks if isinstance(b, dict)]
            print(f"L{n} {str(event.get('timestamp'))[11:19]} {event.get('type')}: {' | '.join(filter(None, parts))}")
    sys.exit()

paths = [p for arg in map(Path, sys.argv[1:]) for p in (sorted(arg.rglob("*.jsonl")) if arg.is_dir() else [arg])]
for path in paths:
    try:
        agent = json.loads(path.with_name(path.stem + ".meta.json").read_text()).get("agentType", "?")
    except (OSError, ValueError, AttributeError):
        agent = "subagent" if "subagents" in path.parts else "session"
    kinds, tools, calls, names = collections.Counter(), collections.Counter(), collections.Counter(), {}
    found = collections.defaultdict(list)
    versions, stamps, bad, n = set(), [], 0, 0
    for n, event in events(path):
        if event is None:
            bad += 1
            continue
        kinds["/".join(str(event[k]) for k in ("type", "subtype") if event.get(k)) or "?"] += 1
        if event.get("version"):
            versions.add(str(event["version"]))
        if isinstance(event.get("timestamp"), str):
            stamps.append(event["timestamp"])
        message = event.get("message") if isinstance(event.get("message"), dict) else {}
        origin = event.get("origin") if isinstance(event.get("origin"), dict) else {}
        if origin.get("handback"):
            found["handbacks received"].append(f"L{n}: {origin.get('name')}: {text(origin.get('handbackReportText'), 300)}")
        elif event.get("type") == "user" and isinstance(message.get("content"), str) and not event.get("isMeta"):
            label = "injected messages" if message["content"].lstrip().startswith("<") else "user prompts"
            found[label].append(f"L{n}: {text(message['content'], 300)}")
        result = event.get("toolUseResult") if isinstance(event.get("toolUseResult"), dict) else {}
        if isinstance(result.get("answers"), dict):
            found["user answers"].append(f"L{n}: {text(list(result['answers'].values()), 300)}")
        if event.get("toolDenialKind"):
            found["denials"].append(f"L{n}: {event['toolDenialKind']}")
        if event.get("hookErrors"):
            found["hook errors"].append(f"L{n}: {text(event['hookErrors'])}")
        for block in dicts(event):
            kind = block.get("type")
            if kind == "tool_use" and isinstance(block.get("name"), str):
                tools[block["name"]] += 1
                names[block.get("id")] = block["name"]
                params = block.get("input") if isinstance(block.get("input"), dict) else {}
                calls[(block["name"], json.dumps(params, sort_keys=True, default=str))] += 1
                if params.get("subagent_type"):
                    found["subagent calls"].append(f"L{n}: {params['subagent_type']}: {text(params.get('description'), 80)}")
                if block["name"] == "SubagentHandback":
                    found["handback sent"].append(f"L{n}: {text(params.get('message'), 300)}")
            elif kind == "tool_result" and block.get("is_error"):
                found["tool errors"].append(f"L{n}: {names.get(block.get('tool_use_id'), '?')}: {text(block.get('content'))}")
            elif kind == "tool_result" and names.get(block.get("tool_use_id")) != "Read" and (hit := FAILED.search(text(block.get("content"), 10**6))):
                found["failures in results"].append(f"L{n}: {names.get(block.get('tool_use_id'), '?')}: ...{hit.group(0)}...")
            elif kind == "text" and "[Request interrupted by user" in str(block.get("text")):
                found["interruptions"].append(f"L{n}")
    repeats = [f"{name} x{count}" for (name, _), count in calls.items() if count >= 3]
    span = f"{min(stamps)} to {max(stamps)}" if stamps else "no timestamps"
    print(f"\n== {path} [{agent}] {n} lines, {bad} unparseable, version {', '.join(sorted(versions)) or '?'}, {span}")
    print("events:", ", ".join(f"{k} x{v}" for k, v in kinds.most_common()))
    print("tools:", ", ".join(f"{k} x{v}" for k, v in tools.most_common()) or "none")
    if repeats:
        print("identical calls repeated 3+ times:", ", ".join(repeats))
    for label, items in found.items():
        print(f"{label} ({len(items)}):")
        for item in items[:40]:
            print("  " + item)
```

## Report

The caller passes this to the user, so lead with what matters most:

- **Evidence:** sessions and subagent runs reviewed, date range, versions, and anything unreadable.
- **Recommendations**, most impactful first. Each with: the problem and its evidence; the root cause; the change, as a diff or exact replacement text with its file path; the expected effect, and the signal the next review checks.
- **Changes to this agent**, in the same format.
- **Earlier recommendations:** the status of each.

=========== SKILL.md
---
name: prd-to-winget-config
description: WinGet configuration procedure (PRD.md to .config/configuration.winget), preloaded into the winget-config-maintainer agent. For any WinGet configuration work, delegate to that agent.
user-invocable: false
---

# PRD to WinGet configuration

`PRD.md` is the source of truth for the user's new Windows 11 PC. Keep `.config/configuration.winget` a traceable translation of it: every requirement is either in the config or in your report, and every unit in the config traces back to a requirement.

`PRD.md` belongs to the user, so you only read it. The config is yours alone, so what's in it now is your last output.

## Steps

1. **Read** `PRD.md` and the config. Done when you have every requirement ID in the PRD and every unit in the config.
   - A requirement ID is uppercase letters, a hyphen and digits, like `APP-01`. The user picks the prefixes.
   - A requirement written without an ID can't be traced, so it stays out of the config and goes in the report under **Needs an ID**.
   - If the PRD has no requirement IDs yet, leave the config as it is and go straight to the report.
2. **Map** each requirement to the unit or units that meet it, using [Resources](#resources). Done when every ID is mapped or has a reason it isn't: unclear, no suitable resource, or outside what a WinGet configuration can do. You can't ask the user anything mid-run, so an unclear requirement stays out of the config and gets one specific question in the report.
3. **Edit** the config to match the mapping. Done when it holds exactly the mapped units, in the order their requirements appear in the PRD. Leave units that are already right byte-for-byte, so the diff shows only real changes.
4. **Check** with the [check script](#checks). Done when it passes, with anything it couldn't verify listed in the report.
5. **Report** as described in [Report](#report).

## File format

Write schema 0.2, the version Microsoft documents. Keep the three header comments and this shape:

```yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://aka.ms/configuration-dsc-schema/0.2
# Maintained by the winget-config-maintainer agent from PRD.md. Change PRD.md, not this file.
# Apply on the PC: winget configure -f .config/configuration.winget
properties:
  assertions:          # preconditions, such as a minimum OS version; only when the PRD asks
    - resource: Microsoft.Windows.Developer/OsVersion
      directives:
        description: "[SYS-01] Require Windows 11"
        allowPrerelease: true
      settings:
        MinVersion: "10.0.22000"
  resources:
    - resource: Microsoft.WinGet.DSC/WinGetPackage
      id: git            # only when another unit lists it in dependsOn
      directives:
        description: "[APP-01] Install Git"
        securityContext: elevated
      settings:
        id: Git.Git
        source: winget
  configurationVersion: 0.2.0
```

Every unit has `directives` and `settings`, and:

- `description` starts with the IDs it serves in square brackets, then a few plain words: `[APP-01] Install Git`, `[APP-02, SET-04] Install VS Code`.
- `securityContext: elevated` when it installs software or changes system-wide settings. WinGet asks for one UAC approval up front, and missing admin rights are the most common reason a configuration fails.
- `allowPrerelease: true` when its module has only prerelease versions on the PowerShell Gallery: today `Microsoft.Windows.Developer` and `Microsoft.Windows.Settings`. `Microsoft.WinGet.DSC` has stable releases.
- `dependsOn` lists the `id`s of units that must succeed first, such as an editor extension that needs the editor.

## Resources

- **Apps:** `Microsoft.WinGet.DSC/WinGetPackage`. Set `id` to the package ID exactly as the check prints it, and `source` to `winget`, or `msstore` for a Microsoft Store app. Leave out `version` unless the PRD pins one; other properties keep their defaults unless a requirement needs them. [Definition](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/winget-cli/master/src/PowerShell/Microsoft.WinGet.DSC/Microsoft.WinGet.DSC.psm1).
- **Windows settings:** Microsoft's winget-dsc modules. Read the resource's class before using it, and copy property names and enum values exactly. Leave `SID` unset: it's a key the resource fills in itself.
  - `Microsoft.Windows.Developer`: DeveloperMode, OsVersion, Taskbar, WindowsExplorer, UserAccessControl, EnableDarkMode, ShowSecondsInClock, EnableRemoteDesktop, EnableLongPathSupport, PowerPlanSetting, WindowsCapability, NetConnectionProfile, AdvancedNetworkSharingSetting, FirewallRule. [Definition](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/winget-dsc/main/resources/Microsoft.Windows.Developer/Microsoft.Windows.Developer.psm1).
  - `Microsoft.Windows.Settings`: WindowsSettings. [Definition](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/winget-dsc/main/resources/Microsoft.Windows.Settings/Microsoft.Windows.Settings.psm1).
- **Anything else** stays out of the config until a resource with a readable definition covers it; give the reason in the report.

## Checks

From the repo root, run `python3 -I .claude/skills/prd-to-winget-config/check.py`. It reads the requirement IDs from `PRD.md` and the package IDs from the config, then checks the config against the schema, that each description cites PRD IDs and each `dependsOn` names a unit, and that each package ID exists, spelled as WinGet or the Store spells it. Passes when it prints `checks: OK` and every ID it lists as not in the config is in your report.

To find package IDs by app name, run it with `--find` and the names: `check.py --find "GOG Galaxy" ubuntu`.

It needs network access and Python 3 with `pyyaml` and `jsonschema`. When it can't run, list what went unchecked in the report.

## Report

End with this report. The caller passes it to the user, so use requirement IDs and plain words:

- **Changes:** units added, changed and removed, each with its IDs, or "No changes."
- **Not in the config:** each ID left out, with its reason.
- **Needs an ID:** requirements written without one.
- **Questions:** one specific question per unclear requirement.
- **Unchecked:** anything a check couldn't verify.

=================== codebase-design/DEEPENING.md
# Deepening

How to deepen a cluster of shallow modules safely, given its dependencies. Assumes the vocabulary in [SKILL.md](SKILL.md): **module**, **interface**, **seam**, **adapter**.

## Dependency categories

When assessing a candidate for deepening, classify its dependencies. The category determines how the deepened module is tested across its seam.

### 1. In-process

Pure computation, in-memory state, no I/O. Always deepenable: merge the modules and test through the new interface directly. No adapter needed.

### 2. Local-substitutable

Dependencies that have local test stand-ins (PGLite for Postgres, in-memory filesystem). Deepenable if the stand-in exists. The deepened module is tested with the stand-in running in the test suite. The seam is internal; no port at the module's external interface.

### 3. Remote but owned (Ports & Adapters)

Your own services across a network boundary (microservices, internal APIs). Define a **port** (interface) at the seam. The deep module owns the logic; the transport is injected as an **adapter**. Tests use an in-memory adapter. Production uses an HTTP/gRPC/queue adapter.

Recommendation shape: *"Define a port at the seam, implement an HTTP adapter for production and an in-memory adapter for testing, so the logic sits in one deep module even though it's deployed across a network."*

### 4. True external (Mock)

Third-party services (Stripe, Twilio, etc.) you don't control. The deepened module takes the external dependency as an injected port; tests provide a mock adapter.

## Seam discipline

- **One adapter means a hypothetical seam. Two adapters means a real one.** Don't introduce a port unless at least two adapters are justified (typically production + test). A single-adapter seam is just indirection.
- **Internal seams vs external seams.** A deep module can have internal seams (private to its implementation, used by its own tests) as well as the external seam at its interface. Don't expose internal seams through the interface just because tests use them.

# Codebase Design

Design **deep modules**: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam, testable through that interface. Use this language and these principles wherever code is being designed or restructured. The aim is leverage for callers, locality for maintainers, and testability for everyone.

## Glossary

Use these terms exactly: don't substitute "component," "service," "API," or "boundary." Consistent language is the whole point.

**Module**: anything with an interface and an implementation. Deliberately scale-agnostic: a function, class, package, or tier-spanning slice. _Avoid_: unit, component, service.

**Interface**: everything a caller must know to use the module correctly: the type signature, but also invariants, ordering constraints, error modes, required configuration, and performance characteristics. _Avoid_: API, signature (too narrow, they refer only to the type-level surface).

**Implementation**: what's inside a module, its body of code. Distinct from **Adapter**: a thing can be a small adapter with a large implementation (a Postgres repo) or a large adapter with a small implementation (an in-memory fake). Reach for "adapter" when the seam is the topic; "implementation" otherwise.

**Depth**: leverage at the interface. The amount of behaviour a caller (or test) can exercise per unit of interface they have to learn. A module is **deep** when a large amount of behaviour sits behind a small interface, **shallow** when the interface is nearly as complex as the implementation.

**Seam** _(Michael Feathers)_: a place where you can alter behaviour without editing in that place; the *location* at which a module's interface lives. Where to put the seam is its own design decision, distinct from what goes behind it. _Avoid_: boundary (overloaded with DDD's bounded context).

**Adapter**: a concrete thing that satisfies an interface at a seam. Describes *role* (what slot it fills), not substance (what's inside).

**Leverage**: what callers get from depth. More capability per unit of interface they learn. One implementation pays back across N call sites and M tests.

**Locality**: what maintainers get from depth. Change, bugs, knowledge, and verification concentrate in one place rather than spreading across callers. Fix once, fixed everywhere.

## Deep vs shallow

**Deep module** = small interface + lots of implementation:

```
┌─────────────────────┐
│   Small Interface   │  ← Few methods, simple params
├─────────────────────┤
│                     │
│  Deep Implementation│  ← Complex logic hidden
│                     │
└─────────────────────┘
```

**Shallow module** = large interface + little implementation (avoid):

```
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│       Large Interface           │  ← Many methods, complex params
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│  Thin Implementation            │  ← Just passes through
└─────────────────────────────────┘
```

When designing an interface, ask:

- Can I reduce the number of methods?
- Can I simplify the parameters?
- Can I hide more complexity inside?

## Principles

- **Depth is a property of the interface, not the implementation.** A deep module can be internally composed of small, mockable, swappable parts; they just aren't part of the interface. - **The interface is the test surface.** Callers and tests cross the same seam. If you want to test *past* the interface, the module is probably the wrong shape.

1. **Accept dependencies, don't create them.**

   // Testable

   function processOrder(order) {

   }
   ```

   ```typescript

   }

- A **Seam** is where a **Module**'s **Interface** lives.

# ADR Format

ADRs live in `docs/adr/` and use sequential numbering: `0001-slug.md`, `0002-slug.md`, etc.

Create the `docs/adr/` directory lazily: only when the first ADR is needed.

## Template

```md
# {Short title of the decision}

{1-3 sentences: what's the context, what did we decide, and why.}
```

That's it. An ADR can be a single paragraph. The value is in recording *that* a decision was made and *why*, not in filling out sections.

## Optional sections

Only include these when they add genuine value. Most ADRs won't need them.

- **Status** frontmatter (`proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded by ADR-NNNN`): useful when decisions are revisited
- **Considered Options**: only when the rejected alternatives are worth remembering
- **Consequences**: only when non-obvious downstream effects need to be called out

## Numbering

Scan `docs/adr/` for the highest existing number and increment by one.

## When to offer an ADR

All three of these must be true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will look at the code and wonder "why on earth did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If a decision is easy to reverse, skip it: you'll just reverse it. If it's not surprising, nobody will wonder why. If there was no real alternative, there's nothing to record beyond "we did the obvious thing."

### What qualifies

- **Architectural shape.** "We're using a monorepo." "The write model is event-sourced, the read model is projected into Postgres."
- **Integration patterns between contexts.** "Ordering and Billing communicate via domain events, not synchronous HTTP."
- **Technology choices that carry lock-in.** Database, message bus, auth provider, deployment target. Not every library: just the ones that would take a quarter to swap out.
- **Boundary and scope decisions.** "Customer data is owned by the Customer context; other contexts reference it by ID only." The explicit no-s are as valuable as the yes-s.
- **Deliberate deviations from the obvious path.** "We're using manual SQL instead of an ORM because X." Anything where a reasonable reader would assume the opposite. These stop the next engineer from "fixing" something that was deliberate.
- **Constraints not visible in the code.** "We can't use AWS because of compliance requirements." "Response times must be under 200ms because of the partner API contract."
- **Rejected alternatives when the rejection is non-obvious.** If you considered GraphQL and picked REST for subtle reasons, record it; otherwise someone will suggest GraphQL again in six months.

# CONTEXT.md Format

## Structure

```md
# {Context Name}

{One or two sentence description of what this context is and why it exists.}

## Language

**Order**:
{A one or two sentence description of the term}
_Avoid_: Purchase, transaction

**Invoice**:
A request for payment sent to a customer after delivery.
_Avoid_: Bill, payment request

**Customer**:
A person or organization that places orders.
_Avoid_: Client, buyer, account
```

## Rules

- **Be opinionated.** When multiple words exist for the same concept, pick the best one and list the others under `_Avoid_`.
- **Keep definitions tight.** One or two sentences max. Define what it IS, not what it does.
- **Only include terms specific to this project's context.** General programming concepts (timeouts, error types, utility patterns) don't belong even if the project uses them extensively. Before adding a term, ask: is this a concept unique to this context, or a general programming concept? Only the former belongs.
- **Group terms under subheadings** when natural clusters emerge. If all terms belong to a single cohesive area, a flat list is fine.

## Single vs multi-context repos

**Single context (most repos):** One `CONTEXT.md` at the repo root.

**Multiple contexts:** A `CONTEXT-MAP.md` at the repo root lists the contexts, where they live, and how they relate to each other:

```md
# Context Map

## Contexts

- [Ordering](./src/ordering/CONTEXT.md): receives and tracks customer orders
- [Billing](./src/billing/CONTEXT.md): generates invoices and processes payments
- [Fulfillment](./src/fulfillment/CONTEXT.md): manages warehouse picking and shipping

## Relationships

- **Ordering → Fulfillment**: Ordering emits `OrderPlaced` events; Fulfillment consumes them to start picking
- **Fulfillment → Billing**: Fulfillment emits `ShipmentDispatched` events; Billing consumes them to generate invoices
- **Ordering ↔ Billing**: Shared types for `CustomerId` and `Money`
```

The skill infers which structure applies:

- If `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists, read it to find contexts
- If only a root `CONTEXT.md` exists, single context
- If neither exists, create a root `CONTEXT.md` lazily when the first term is resolved

When multiple contexts exist, infer which one the current topic relates to. If unclear, ask.

│   └── adr/

└── src/
```

```

├── CONTEXT-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── CONTEXT.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/

│       └── docs/adr/
```

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `CONTEXT.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

When a term is resolved, update `CONTEXT.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [CONTEXT-FORMAT.md](./CONTEXT-FORMAT.md).

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

# Deepening

How to deepen a cluster of shallow modules safely, given its dependencies. Assumes the vocabulary in [SKILL.md](SKILL.md): **module**, **interface**, **seam**, **adapter**.

## Dependency categories

When assessing a candidate for deepening, classify its dependencies. The category determines how the deepened module is tested across its seam.

### 1. In-process

Pure computation, in-memory state, no I/O. Always deepenable: merge the modules and test through the new interface directly. No adapter needed.

### 2. Local-substitutable

Dependencies that have local test stand-ins (PGLite for Postgres, in-memory filesystem). Deepenable if the stand-in exists. The deepened module is tested with the stand-in running in the test suite. The seam is internal; no port at the module's external interface.

### 3. Remote but owned (Ports & Adapters)

Your own services across a network boundary (microservices, internal APIs). Define a **port** (interface) at the seam. The deep module owns the logic; the transport is injected as an **adapter**. Tests use an in-memory adapter. Production uses an HTTP/gRPC/queue adapter.

Third-party services (Stripe, Twilio, etc.) you don't control. The deepened module takes the external dependency as an injected port; tests provide a mock adapter.

- **One adapter means a hypothetical seam. Two adapters means a real one.** Don't introduce a port unless at least two adapters are justified (typically production + test). A single-adapter seam is just indirection.
- **Internal seams vs external seams.** A deep module can have internal seams (private to its implementation, used by its own tests) as well as the external seam at its interface. Don't expose internal seams through the interface just because tests use them.

- **Integration patterns between contexts.** "Ordering and Billing communicate via domain events, not synchronous HTTP."
- **Technology choices that carry lock-in.** Database, message bus, auth provider, deployment target. Not every library: just the ones that would take a quarter to swap out.
- **Boundary and scope decisions.** "Customer data is owned by the Customer context; other contexts reference it by ID only." The explicit no-s are as valuable as the yes-s.
- **Deliberate deviations from the obvious path.** "We're using manual SQL instead of an ORM because X." Anything where a reasonable reader would assume the opposite. These stop the next engineer from "fixing" something that was deliberate.
- **Constraints not visible in the code.** "We can't use AWS because of compliance requirements." "Response times must be under 200ms because of the partner API contract."
- **Rejected alternatives when the rejection is non-obvious.** If you considered GraphQL and picked REST for subtle reasons, record it; otherwise someone will suggest GraphQL again in six months.

=================== domain-modeling/CONTEXT-FORMAT.md
# CONTEXT.md Format

## Structure

```md
# {Context Name}

{One or two sentence description of what this context is and why it exists.}

## Language

**Order**:
{A one or two sentence description of the term}
_Avoid_: Purchase, transaction

**Invoice**:
A request for payment sent to a customer after delivery.
_Avoid_: Bill, payment request

**Customer**:
A person or organization that places orders.
_Avoid_: Client, buyer, account
```

## Rules

- **Be opinionated.** When multiple words exist for the same concept, pick the best one and list the others under `_Avoid_`.
- **Keep definitions tight.** One or two sentences max. Define what it IS, not what it does.
- **Only include terms specific to this project's context.** General programming concepts (timeouts, error types, utility patterns) don't belong even if the project uses them extensively. Before adding a term, ask: is this a concept unique to this context, or a general programming concept? Only the former belongs.
- **Group terms under subheadings** when natural clusters emerge. If all terms belong to a single cohesive area, a flat list is fine.

## Single vs multi-context repos

**Single context (most repos):** One `CONTEXT.md` at the repo root.

**Multiple contexts:** A `CONTEXT-MAP.md` at the repo root lists the contexts, where they live, and how they relate to each other:

```md
# Context Map

## Contexts

- [Ordering](./src/ordering/CONTEXT.md): receives and tracks customer orders
- [Billing](./src/billing/CONTEXT.md): generates invoices and processes payments
- [Fulfillment](./src/fulfillment/CONTEXT.md): manages warehouse picking and shipping

## Relationships

- **Ordering → Fulfillment**: Ordering emits `OrderPlaced` events; Fulfillment consumes them to start picking
- **Fulfillment → Billing**: Fulfillment emits `ShipmentDispatched` events; Billing consumes them to generate invoices
- **Ordering ↔ Billing**: Shared types for `CustomerId` and `Money`
```

The skill infers which structure applies:

- If `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists, read it to find contexts
- If only a root `CONTEXT.md` exists, single context
- If neither exists, create a root `CONTEXT.md` lazily when the first term is resolved

When multiple contexts exist, infer which one the current topic relates to. If unclear, ask.

=================== domain-modeling/SKILL.md
---
name: domain-modeling
description: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when discussing codebase terminology, writing or editing a CONTEXT.md, or recording or editing an ADR.
---

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `CONTEXT.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── CONTEXT.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── CONTEXT-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── CONTEXT.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── CONTEXT.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `CONTEXT.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `CONTEXT.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

### Update CONTEXT.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `CONTEXT.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [CONTEXT-FORMAT.md](./CONTEXT-FORMAT.md).

`CONTEXT.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `CONTEXT.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

Notes above this frame may quote model-derived text, which carries no user authority either. The report follows:
  Kiro steering and specs docs, read from kiro.dev. The primary steering URL worked, so the fallback was not needed.
  
  Pages read:
  - https://kiro.dev/docs/steering/ (HTTP 200, "Page updated: October 21, 2026")
  - https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/concepts (HTTP 404 Not Found). This is a permanent failure, so sending it again would fail the same way. The Specs navigation I fetched lists no concepts page.
  - Substitutes, both linked from Kiro's own navigation: https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/ (HTTP 200, "Page updated: October 15, 2026") and https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/feature-specs/ (HTTP 200, "Page updated: August 4, 2026").
  
  1. What steering files are, where they live, and the foundational files
  - Definition: "Steering gives Kiro persistent knowledge about your project through markdown files."
  - Workspace steering lives in `.kiro/steering/` under the project root: "Workspace steering files reside in your project root folder under `.kiro/steering/`, and apply only to that specific workspace."
  - Global steering lives in `~/.kiro/steering/` and applies to all workspaces. On conflicts: "Kiro will prioritize the workspace steering instructions." The capability table lists global steering for IDE and CLI only, not Web or Mobile.
  - Foundation ("project steering") files. In the IDE, the "Generate Steering Docs" button, or the "+" button then "Foundation steering files", creates them in `.kiro/steering/`. The table lists this UI generation as IDE-only.
    - `product.md` (Product Overview): "Defines your product's purpose, target users, key features, and business objectives."
    - `tech.md` (Technology Stack): "Documents your chosen frameworks, libraries, development tools, and technical constraints."
    - `structure.md` (Project Structure): "Outlines file organization, naming conventions, import patterns, and architectural decisions."
    - "These foundation files are included in every interaction by default, forming the baseline of Kiro's project understanding."
  
  2. Build guidance versus what is needed
  Steering is mainly about how the solution is built. `tech.md` covers stack and tooling, and `structure.md` covers organization, naming, imports and architectural decisions. The custom-file examples follow the same pattern: `code-conventions.md` specifies "naming patterns, file organization, import ordering, and architectural decisions." The exception is `product.md`, which gives product context that helps Kiro understand "the 'why' behind technical decisions." The steering page does not itself contrast steering with requirements. Per-feature "what is needed" lives in the Specs requirements.md (see below).
  
  3. Inclusion modes

content.text:
The scaffold does a good job of saying what each file is and who owns it. Its biggest gaps are about what happens over time: how anyone knows the implementation works, how a change moves through the files, and where decisions get remembered. I haven't changed anything.

### Bigger gaps

**1. Nothing says how anyone knows the implementation works.** The human isn't expected to understand the implementation, so evidence that it works is their only assurance.
- **Who checks what:** the V-model pairs each level of requirements with a level of checking. Boehm's split maps onto your ownership: *validation* ("is this what's needed?") is the human's, against the top level. *Verification* ("does it do what's written?") is the agent's, through the contract.
- **How a requirement states its test:** Volere's *fit criteria* and Spec Kit's success criteria ("technology-agnostic and measurable") let a requirement carry its own test without naming a solution. EARS and Given/When/Then are common formats.
- **Who fixes a defect:** either the implementation misses a requirement (the agent fixes it), or the requirements miss a need (the human fixes them).

→ New section: **Verification**. It touches #2's open question on citing IDs in the implementation, so it would say *that* each requirement is verified, not how.

**2. Nothing covers change.** The scaffold describes the files at rest.
- **Downward:** a change flows along the diagram's arrows. Edit a requirement, and its children, the contract, the implementation and its verification all need re-checking. Requirements tools call these "suspect links".
- **Upward:** building the solution teaches you about the problem (Nuseibeh's "Twin Peaks"). So a conflict an agent finds goes into an issue, never into a quiet workaround in the implementation. That's a rule about the repo, so it fits the scope you set when you took out "stop and ask".

→ New section: **When something changes**. #2's open questions on permanent IDs and removals would also end up here.

**3. The solution space has no memory.** Agents start each session blank, the human doesn't read the implementation, and transcripts are a raw log. Nothing records why the agent chose its technology, or its reasons for departing from a `FAVOR`.
- **Decision records:** Architecture Decision Records (Nygard) are the standard fix. Your domain-modeling skill already has a short format: `docs/adr/`, only for decisions that are hard to reverse, surprising, and "a real trade-off".
- **Spec Kit's version:** a plan must pass a "Constitution Check", and violations it justifies go in a table. That's close to your stated reasons for departing.
- **Next to transcripts:** transcripts are the log, ADRs the condensed record.

→ New section: **Decision records**, once #2 settles where departure reasons go.

**4. Ownership doesn't yet tell an agent what it may edit.**
- **Ideas or keystrokes?** "Comes entirely from the human" is ambiguous, and agents do nearly all the typing here. I'd make it about ideas: an agent may write the human's points into a human-owned file, never its own.
- **Unlisted files:** `save-transcript.sh` is in the tree but has no owner, and an agent can't tell whether an unlisted file is the implementation. The *fail-safe defaults* principle (Saltzer and Schroeder) says unlisted means not the agent's. A fixed folder for the implementation, with a name that says nothing about technology, would settle this without "every other file".
- **Agent roles:** #2 gives the example of keeping the implementing agent out of shared files, but the definitions treat all agents alike. Each kind could say what an agent may write:
  - human-owned: the human's own points
  - shared: what the human has agreed
  - agent-owned: anything within the rules
- **Mixed ownership in one file:** `REQUIREMENTS.md` changes owner below its top level. Hooks and CODEOWNERS enforce by file path, so they can't enforce a split inside one file.

**5. The problem space only has room for needs.**
- **Assumptions:** Michael Jackson's "The World and the Machine" is the classic theory behind your split. It separates what's wanted (requirements) from what's true of the world anyway (domain assumptions). The specification sits between them, roughly your contract, and a design is right when the specification plus the assumptions guarantee the requirements. The scaffold has no home for assumptions, so they'll leak into the requirements or the steering.
- **Constraints:** Volere's template has separate sections for "Relevant Facts and Assumptions" and "Mandated Constraints". In your model, mandated constraints are `ALWAYS`/`NEVER`, which is worth saying outright.
- **A test for agents:** from Parnas's information hiding, "if the technology were swapped out, would this line change? Then it's solution space."

→ New sections: **Telling the spaces apart** and **Assumptions**.

**6. The file could build the comprehension debt it warns about.** The contract shows up in as many as seven places: the glossary, its section, the table, the diagram and three analogies. Your meta-reviewer's own rule is "each rule lives in one place". Two fixes:
- Say which wins when they disagree. The text sets the rules, the glossary defines terms, and the diagram and analogies only illustrate, the way RFCs separate binding text from explanation.
- Make the analogies one table, with a row per part and a column per analogy. It keeps the coverage you asked for, shows gaps at a glance, and is much shorter.

**7. Some rules live only in issues.** When issue 3 closes, these go with it:
- Say "human" and "agent", never "you".
- Files state what's agreed now, not how it got there.
- Examples appear only as unrelated analogies.

Since all work starts from an issue, the issue's layout (Out of scope, Done when, Audit trail) is also an unwritten template. You kept conventions out in the first grilling round, but these would otherwise be lost. Nothing tells an agent the branch setup either: the default branch is `blank`, and work lands on `win11-winget-config`.

→ New section: **Writing conventions**.

**8. No rule is backed by a check.** Your meta-reviewer says a rule broken in prose gets "enforced by mechanism". *Fitness functions* (Ford, Parsons and Kua) are the established form of that. These could be checked:
- Each requirement cites a parent ID that exists.
- Each steering bullet starts with a keyword.
- Each commit has `Issue:` and `Transcript:` lines.
- Glossary synonyms don't appear. Vale lints prose against a word list.
- No requirement names a technology, via an LLM check.

→ New section: **Before committing**, a Definition of Done that points to the other sections instead of repeating them.

**9. The audit trail needs a privacy rule, and has two gaps.** Every turn is pushed to a public branch, so anything an agent reads or prints can become public. The last session found your email in 20 transcripts.
- A commit the human makes alone has no transcript to link.
- Links to the branch keep changing as a session grows, unlike #2's links pinned to a commit.

→ New section: **Secrets and privacy**.

### Frameworks that sharpen what's there

- **Spec-driven development** (GitHub Spec Kit, Kiro) is the closest modern relative of your whole design. Kiro even calls its agent guidance "steering", though it mixes in product context, which your split keeps out. Gaps 1, 3 and 5 are parts these tools have and the scaffold doesn't.
- **RFC 2119** matches your steering keywords almost one-to-one. `ALWAYS`/`NEVER` are MUST/MUST NOT, `FAVOR`/`DISFAVOR` are SHOULD/SHOULD NOT, and `CONSIDER` is MAY. RFC 8174 even makes the words count only in capitals, like yours. Citing it gives agents a meaning they already know. Yours is stricter in one useful way: a departure gets written down.
- **Design by Contract** (Meyer): the `.pyi` analogy implies the contract is signatures only. Your codebase-design skill defines an interface more broadly: everything a caller must know, including invariants, error modes and required configuration. It calls "signature" too narrow. Worth deciding whether the contract covers preconditions and what happens on failure.
- **Goal-oriented requirements engineering** (KAOS): your tree is a goal refinement tree, where asking "why?" moves up and "how?" moves down. It raises a question the scaffold doesn't answer: can a requirement serve two parents?
- **INCOSE's guide and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148** list the qualities of a good requirement. The scaffold already demands solution-free. It doesn't ask for singular (one need per line), verifiable or feasible. "Can't be verified as stated" also works as the rule for when to break a requirement down.
- **More DDD:**
  - *Bounded contexts:* the glossary holds the method's terms. The PC's own terms will need a home too, in the problem space.
  - *Avoid* lines under each term, as your domain-modeling skill's format has.
  - "Trace" currently means two things: requirements tracing back to the top, and the audit trail.
  - That skill creates a `CONTEXT.md` when none exists, so name `GLOSSARY.md` as the only glossary.
- **AGENTS.md:** since September 2026 (v2.1.277), Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md` when there's no `CLAUDE.md` in the folder or above it. The pointer could be `AGENTS.md`, which Codex, Cursor, Copilot and Kiro also read. That fits #2's technology-neutral goal, but it changes issue 3.

### Where the new sections would sit

```
  ## The two spaces
+ ### Telling the spaces apart
  ## Problem space files
  ### Requirements
+ ### Assumptions
  ## Boundary files
  ## Solution space files
  ### Steering
  ### Implementation
+ ### Decision records
+ ## Verification
+ ## When something changes
  ## Analogies (one table)
  ## Traceability
+ ## Writing conventions
+ ## Before committing
+ ## Secrets and privacy
```

I'd add Verification, the ownership rules and When something changes first. Which would you like to dig into? I can also put this review on a page if you'd rather comment on it there.

Sources: [Spec Kit spec template](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/github/spec-kit/main/templates/spec-template.md), [Spec Kit plan template](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/github/spec-kit/main/templates/plan-template.md), [Kiro steering](https://kiro.dev/docs/steering/), [Kiro feature specs](https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/feature-specs/), [Claude Code docs on AGENTS.md](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory), [Simon Willison on the AGENTS.md announcement](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Sep/18/thariq-shihipar/), [paper summarizing the ISO 29148 criteria](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.10886)
